_meta: A case-insensitive blocklist check and three inputs, used to show why converting case with a locale-sensitive rule (lower/upper as the OS locale defines them) makes the same code behave differently on different machines -- the classic Turkish-I problem -- and why case-insensitive comparison must use a locale-independent case fold. Uppercase/lowercase mapping is not universal: it depends on the locale. The most famous divergence is the letter I. In most locales the uppercase 'I' lowercases to 'i' (dotted), but in Turkish and Azeri locales the alphabet has two separate I letters -- a dotless I ('I'/'ı') and a dotted one ('İ'/'i') -- so 'I' lowercases to 'ı' (dotless) and it is 'İ' that lowercases to 'i'. Any comparison that lowercases (or uppercases) strings using the machine's locale therefore gets a different answer depending on where it runs. This breaks case-insensitive checks silently and dangerously: a blocklist that lowercases the input and compares it to 'admin' matches 'ADMIN' on a machine in an English locale (ADMIN -> admin) but NOT on a machine in a Turkish locale (ADMIN -> admın, with a dotless i), so the forbidden name sails through -- same code, different security behavior by locale. The fix is a locale-independent case fold (invariant casing): fold case by the fixed Unicode default mapping, not the OS locale, so the comparison gives the same result on every machine. forbidden is the name the check should reject case-insensitively; inputs are the strings to test. invariant_lower and turkish_lower model the two locale mappings applied character by character. forbidden and inputs are the fixture; every lowercased form and every block decision under each locale are computed.
